when_to_use: When you want to pull data from a new website or domain, you need to get a human's okay in the dashboard before the system can fetch it. Use this for any first‑time URL access.
Use this when you need to solve basic addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division in your head because calculators, pens, or other aids aren’t allowed.
When you want to keep something in memory but only after you’ve pulled it from a website or opened a file you already have.
When you want to convert the raw token count into the real‑world amount by adjusting for the asset’s decimal precision. Useful for showing balances or calculating values in everyday terms.
When you are creating a short overview of news feeds and need to list the original article titles as references.
Use this when you need a JSON object on a single line with no extra spaces or line breaks, such as for a tiny config, embedding in a URL, or sending a compact payload.
Use this when you need to find out how many bytes a single emoji occupies, such as checking file size limits or counting storage space for text that includes emojis.
Use this whenever you need to replace the entire contents of a file with new data instead of appending to what’s already there, such as when you want to completely refresh a text file.
When you need to generate a tiny piece of text that must be exactly five bytes in size, for example creating a very small file or verifying a byte count.
Use this when you need to see every file inside a folder hierarchy, including those in subfolders, after adding new files. It’s handy for scanning a directory tree to retrieve all file paths.

Use this when you’re saving or referencing a file with a path that includes ‘./’ or other dot segments, and you need to know that the system will clean the path and still write the file in the intended folder.

When you need to create an empty file or confirm that writing no content results in a file of size zero. Use it for generating placeholder files or checking that a file‑writing operation reports 0 bytes for empty input.

When you need to save a file into a new subfolder chain and expect the system to create the directories automatically, without running a separate make‑folder command. Handy for generating output files in deep directories on the fly.
Use this when someone asks for the contents of a file that isn’t present, or when a file‑reading operation fails because the file is missing.
When you need each document to include its own filename inside its text, and you must look at a specific file before responding.
When you need to raise a numeric value stored in a plain text file by repeatedly reading, adding one, and writing it back, such as updating a simple counter.
When you want to save a file but the target folder may not exist yet, or when you need to refer to a location using a relative path like '..' inside the project.
When a configuration file is missing or cannot be opened, create a default settings file (such as setting the theme to dark) and then load it to retrieve the needed value.
When you want to view every file inside a folder, including those hidden in its subfolders, or need a full inventory of all items in a directory tree.

When you want to add a new line to an existing text file, like a log, without losing its current contents—read the file, keep the old lines, and write back the whole content with the new line at the end.
Use this when you need to determine the byte length of UTF‑8 text (e.g., checking file size or handling raw bytes) instead of counting characters.
